keyVerseText: But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun אֱלוֹהַּ (ʼĕlôwahh) is likely an emphatic or prolonged form derived from the root word אֵל (ʼêl), which conveys strength, might, and power. While commonly translated as 'God,' this root sense emphasizes the divine as a mighty and powerful being, not merely a generic deity. This etymology enriches the English understanding by highlighting God's supreme strength and authority beyond the simple title 'God.'
usageInScripture: Appearing 57 times, אֱלוֹהַּ is primarily translated as 'God' in most contexts, with 10 occurrences explicitly rendered so, and frequently appears in phrases like 'of God' and 'unto God.' Its usage spans references to the true God as well as false gods, indicating a range that includes both the supreme Deity and idols or heathen deities. This dual application reveals the term's flexibility in Hebrew scripture, distinguishing between the one true God and other so-called gods, while always carrying the sense of divine or supernatural power.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding אֱלוֹהַּ in its original Hebrew context deepens our grasp of God's nature as not only the singular Creator but the Almighty with unmatched power and authority. This term's connection to the root אֵל underscores God's might and sovereignty, foundational to evangelical faith which affirms God's unique status above all false gods. Recognizing that the word can also refer to false gods reminds believers of the biblical tension between true worship and idolatry, reinforcing the call to exclusive devotion to the one true God. Thus, the term anchors Christian theology in the reality of God's transcendent strength and the necessity of faithful allegiance to Him alone.
keyVerseReflection: Deuteronomy 32:15 speaks of Jeshurun becoming complacent and forsaking 'God which made him,' highlighting the relationship between the people and their Creator. The use of אֱלוֹהַּ here underscores that it is the mighty God—the source of life and salvation—who is being abandoned. This word enriches the verse by reminding readers that the one forsaken is not a mere deity but the powerful, life-giving Rock, emphasizing the seriousness of turning away from the true God.
